content.p: Before dawn on 13 February 1692, soldiers who had spent almost two weeks eating at the fires of the MacDonalds of Glencoe rose from their beds and began to kill their hosts. The victims were a small Highland clan, targeted by the government because their chief was late with his oath. The killers were men of a government regiment, acting on written orders that said they came by the king's special command.

Several accounts give 38 men, women and children killed outright, though the figure is given as about 30 by one museum and as nearly forty by another. Many more fled into a winter storm, and what happened to them is disputed. A commission and the Scottish Parliament later called the killings murder, but nobody was ever punished in court. The case has lasted not because of the numbers but because of the way it was done: Highland custom treated a guest who killed his host as committing something worse than ordinary murder.

The glen's troubles began with a change of kings. James VII of Scotland, who was also James II of England, had alienated his Protestant subjects by favouring Catholics, and in 1688 William of Orange and his wife Mary were invited to take the thrones. Many Highland clans stayed loyal to James and rose in his name, winning at Killiecrankie in 1689 but losing momentum when their leader, Viscount Dundee, was killed. The Glencoe Museum describes a country divided by religion, dynasty and law, and a Highlands where the old clan order was giving way.

In August 1691 William offered the rebel clans a pardon, if their chiefs swore an oath of allegiance before 1 January 1692. The offer carried a threat: those who refused would face "the utmost extremity of the law". The new garrison at Inverlochy, now Fort William, made the threat credible. James, in exile in France, eventually released the chiefs from their loyalty to him, and the news reached the MacDonalds of Glencoe on 29 December 1691, according to the Glencoe Museum.

Their chief, Alasdair MacIain, set out at once, and that is where the story turns on small delays. According to English Monarchs, he reached Fort William on 31 December and was told the oath could only be taken before a sheriff, the nearest being at Inveraray. He was given a letter of protection and a letter asking Sir Colin Campbell, sheriff of Argyll, to accept the oath since he had come within the time allowed. The same source says the journey took three days because of the winter weather and because MacIain was detained at Barcaldine Castle, and that the sheriff was spending the New Year with his family.

The accounts differ on the exact dates. The Glencoe Museum says MacIain reached Inveraray on 2 January and that the sheriff came back three days later. The glen-coe.com history and English Monarchs both say he swore the oath on 6 January, which glen-coe.com calls six days late. The Glencoe Museum says the sheriff was at first reluctant to take it, and that MacIain went home confident that he and his clan were protected; English Monarchs says he was given assurances that his allegiance would be accepted.
content.h2: The minister who wanted an example
content.p: In Edinburgh, the man in charge of Scottish affairs saw it differently. Sir John Dalrymple, Master of Stair, was Secretary of State for Scotland, a Lowlander and a Protestant who, in the words of English Monarchs, despised the "lawless clans". The Glencoe Museum quotes a letter in which he wrote that he rejoiced that MacDonald of Glencoe had not taken the oath: "It is a great work of charity to be exact in rooting out that damnable sept, the worst of the Highlands."

The sources offer several reasons why Glencoe was picked. The Glencoe Museum points to the MacDonalds' reputation for raiding and cattle theft, their mostly Catholic and Jacobite sympathies, and their isolated glen with few ways out. glen-coe.com stresses that they were a small clan with few political allies. English Monarchs says MacIain's certificate of his late oath was sent to Edinburgh but that the government was not properly told he had taken it. Glen-coe.com says Dalrymple obtained orders signed by the King himself.

The choice of regiment has often been read as clan revenge. The Earl of Argyll's Regiment of Foot, and Robert Campbell of Glenlyon, who commanded the detachment, bore the name of the MacDonalds' old rivals. The Clan Campbell Society's history of the two clans traces the rivalry back to the Middle Ages, and puts its root in loyalty to the Scottish crown, with the Campbells upholding royal authority in the west and Clan Donald often resisting it. But the Glencoe Museum says there were only 12 Campbells in the regiment, and English Monarchs says only a minority of the men, who came mostly from the Argyll estates, were Campbells, with many officers from the Lowlands. The Clan Campbell Society says that in 1689 the Glencoe MacIains and the Glengarry Macdonells looted Glenlyon and stole his livestock, though in his appeal for compensation he blamed the Glengarry men more and made no mention of Glencoe. The Glencoe Museum, for its part, says only that Glenlyon had been a victim of a MacDonald raid a few years earlier.

The soldiers arrived in Glencoe at the end of January or on 1 February. The Glencoe Museum puts them at around 130 and glen-coe.com at 120, which is also the figure the BBC gives. They carried papers saying they were collecting arrears of tax and needed billets.

The MacDonalds, who took the soldiers' arrival as one more test of their loyalty, took them in. Highland custom bound them to shelter and feed strangers, and for about two weeks the soldiers shared the families' scarce winter food and drink. The Glencoe Museum records stories of ceilidhs, shinty and even romances. According to the Clan Campbell Society, Glenlyon visited the home of the chief's youngest son, Alexander, whose wife was Glenlyon's niece.
content.h2: The order and the night of 12 February
content.p: On the evening of 12 February Captain Drummond arrived with a written order for Glenlyon from Major Duncanson. The text, as the Clan Campbell Society prints it, directs him to "fall upon the rebels, the McDonalds of Glenco, and put all to the sword under seventy", with "a special care" that "the old Fox and his sons" should not escape and with all the avenues secured. It tells him to act at five in the morning, says Duncanson will try to arrive with a stronger party but that Glenlyon must not wait for him, and declares the order to be "by the Kings speciall command", warning that otherwise he could expect to be "dealt with as one not true to King nor Government". The Glencoe Museum adds that two more regiments were placed near Ballachulish and Kinlochleven to close the escape routes.
English Monarchs says Drummond spent that evening playing cards with the men he was ordered to kill and accepted an invitation to dine with the chief the next day.

The attack began at about five o'clock in settlements along the glen, though the killing spread wherever people ran. MacIain was shot as he got out of bed. English Monarchs names Lt Lindsay and Ensign Lundie as the men who killed him, and says his wife was stripped and died the next day on the mountainside; glen-coe.com adds that she was stripped of her rings. English Monarchs records that the first clansman to die, Duncan Rankin, was shot while trying to cross the River Coe, and says some captives were bound hand and foot before being killed. Houses were set on fire.

How many died depends on who is counting. The figure of 38 killed appears in the Glencoe Museum and glen-coe.com; the West Highland Museum says 30; English Monarchs says "nearly forty".The Glencoe Museum says houses were torched and that women, children and the elderly were driven out into the snow, with many dying of exposure. glen-coe.com says perhaps 300 people fled into the mountains in the blizzard and that an unknown number died there. The two totals cannot be added up from these pages.

Many escaped. MacIain's sons John and Alexander led survivors across Meall Mor to Appin, where the Stewarts sheltered them, according to the Glencoe Museum. Others hid in Coire Gabhail, the Hidden Valley, or went down to Glen Etive. The West Highland Museum holds a small digging tool said by its donor to have been carried to Glen Creran by a party who broke out of the back of a house as the soldiers came in at the front.

The sources suggest that the soldiers' own hesitation helped. The Glencoe Museum says there are many stories of whispered warnings and of men firing over the heads of those they were told to hunt. English Monarchs names two lieutenants, Francis Farquhar and Gilbert Kennedy, who snapped their swords instead of obeying; they were arrested and jailed, then cleared and freed. glen-coe.com says troops from Fort William, who were meant to close the ring around the glen, did not arrive in time, and that otherwise far more would have died.
content.h2: The inquiry and who was blamed
content.p: Public outrage grew. The Glencoe Museum says Jacobites produced pamphlets that carried the story as far as London, that survivors and soldiers told what they had seen, and that Glenlyon is claimed to have leaked the order he received. In the summer of 1695 the Scottish Parliament conducted an inquiry. According to glen-coe.com the inquiry found the killings to be "murder under trust", a category in Scots law considered worse than ordinary murder.

The West Highland Museum says that, because the orders came from the king, the inquiry did not ask whether they were lawful but whether the men had gone beyond them. English Monarchs says the commission's report declared the attack murder but exonerated the king, with most of the blame placed on Dalrymple; Parliament voted that it was murder and named those it held responsible, and William was asked directly to bring them to justice but did nothing. glen-coe.com puts it bluntly: the inquiry recommended only that Dalrymple be prosecuted, he never was, and no one was punished.

The Glencoe Museum says that Dalrymple was forced to resign but was later reinstated in a higher post and had a hand in negotiating the Acts of Union before he died, and that Glenlyon stayed in the army, served in Flanders and died in poverty in Bruges in 1696. It also says it is unclear whether William knew the full extent of the orders he signed, and that he escaped blame by saying his instruction had been interpreted too zealously.
content.h2: Memory, myth and the glen today
content.p: The massacre was meant to cow the clans. According to the Glencoe Museum it did the opposite, hardening Highland feeling against the government. The Glencoe Museum says that because Glenlyon was involved, the massacre is often wrongly remembered as clan-on-clan violence, a continuation of the feud between the MacDonalds and the Campbells.

The memorial is a Celtic cross on a cairn at the eastern end of Glencoe village, put up in 1883 by a MacDonald of Aberdeen, according to English Monarchs. glen-coe.com says that every 13 February members of Clan Donald gather there to lay wreaths.

The survivors did return. glen-coe.com says they rebuilt and the clan continued, diminished but unbroken. In October 2023 the BBC reported that archaeologists from the University of Glasgow had found 36 coins in a pot buried under a hearth stone at the site of a house associated with MacIain, in a side glen where people fled in the storm. None were minted after the 1680s, and whoever hid them did not come back for them, which led the archaeologists to suggest they were hidden just before or during the killings, and that whoever buried them, who did not return for them, may have been among the victims. That is the archaeologists' suggestion; it is not proof. The same excavation found everyday objects such as spindle whorls, a pitchfork and a dress pin, which the dig's director said showed the lives of the people who worked the land there.
